title: Chapter 2: Principles of Toxicology
source: Casarett & Doull's Toxicology: The Basic Science of Poisons, 9th edition, Chapter 2 (Lauren M. Aleksunes; David L. Eaton)
file: Casarett and Doull’s Toxicology Chapter 2: Principles of Toxicology
lecture: 10/9 (Principles of Toxicology; finished 10/13). Syllabus: read through the Variation in Toxic Responses section.
about: Toxicology is the study of the adverse effects of chemical, biological, or physical agents on living organisms and the environment, and the chapter opens by distinguishing toxins, xenobiotics and toxicants and by stating that the dose makes the poison, with Table 2-1 giving approximate acute LD50 values. It describes the subdisciplines of toxicology, the spectrum of undesired effects (allergic and idiosyncratic reactions, immediate versus delayed, reversible versus irreversible, local versus systemic toxicity, chemical interactions and tolerance), and the characteristics of exposure (route and site; acute, subacute, subchronic and chronic duration; frequency relative to elimination half-life). The relationship between dose and response is the foundation of modern toxicology, and the chapter covers individual (graded) and quantal (population) dose-response relationships, the LD50 and threshold dose, probit transformation, dose extrapolation across species, monotonic and nonmonotonic curve shapes (threshold versus linear nonthreshold models, essential nutrients, hormesis, endocrine active chemicals), and the therapeutic index, margin of safety, margin of exposure, potency and efficacy. It then discusses causation in toxicology, mechanisms and modes of action, adverse outcome pathways, and variation in toxic responses due to selective toxicity, species differences and modifying factors (genetics, age, sex, circadian rhythm, microbiome). The remainder of the chapter describes toxicity testing (acute through chronic, developmental, mutagenicity, carcinogenicity, neurotoxicity, immunotoxicity, sensitization, irritation) and systems toxicology (omics, exposome, high-content screening, computational toxicology, innovative testing models).

terms.chapter_definition: The study of the adverse effects of chemical, biological, or physical agents on living organisms and the environment.
The dose (mg/kg body weight) causing death in 50% of exposed animals; where death is the measured endpoint, the ED50 is referred to as the lethal dose LD50.

Acute exposure refers to exposure to a chemical for less than 24 hours; subacute exposure refers to repeated exposure for 1 month or less, subchronic for 1 to 3 months, and chronic for more than 3 months.
Time necessary for 50% of the chemical to be removed from the bloodstream.
Describes the response of an individual organism to increasing doses of a chemical, often referred to as a 'graded' response because the measured effect is continuous over a range of doses.

Characterizes the distribution of individual responses to different doses in a population of organisms; quantal, or 'all or none', in nature: at any given dose an individual is classified as either a 'responder' or a 'nonresponder'.

The minimal ED of any chemical that evokes a stated all-or-none response; a threshold is a dose at which toxicity is first observed, and at doses below this level the probability of an individual responding is zero.
Assumes there is a direct and proportional relationship between dose and response, even at very low doses; this extrapolation is typically performed for genotoxic carcinogens.
Some non-nutritional toxic substances may impart beneficial or stimulatory effects at low doses but, at higher doses, produce adverse effects.
The ratio of the dose required to cause a toxic effect to the dose needed to produce the desired therapeutic response; most commonly the median doses TD50 and ED50.

Calculated from the ED99 for the desired effect and the TD1 for the undesired effect; for nondrug chemicals, an indicator of the magnitude of the difference between an estimated exposed dose and the NOAEL.
Compares the estimated daily exposure, in milligrams per kilogram per day, with some estimated value from the quantal dose-response relationship (e.g., NOAEL or TD10), expressed as a ratio.

listen: This reading is Chapter two, Principles of Toxicology, by Lauren Aleksunes and David Eaton, in Casarett and Doull's Toxicology, The Basic Science of Poisons, ninth edition. She called it a textbook that toxicologists use all the time, and her Principles of Toxicology lecture took its tables and figures from it. Table two dash one lists acute L D fifty values in rats, the dose that kills half the animals. Ethyl alcohol is ten thousand milligrams per kilogram. Botulinum toxin is zero point zero zero zero zero one milligrams per kilogram. She said the dose makes the poison, but you have to know what compound you're talking about too. Figure two dash three sets the exposure periods for animal studies. Acute is less than twenty four hours. Subacute is one month or less. Subchronic is one to three months. Chronic is more than three months. Figure two dash four gives compounds A, B and C in repeated doses. A, with the longest half life, is toxic by the third dose, and B by about the fourth or fifth. C clears quickly and never reaches the toxic zone. Even so, a compound cleared before the next exposure may still cause chronic adverse effects, which her key marks true. Her reasons were an allergic response, a different target site, synergy with other drugs, and damage at an injection site. A graded response is one individual's continuous response to increasing doses. A quantal response is all or none, across a population, and Figure two dash six uses it to find the L D fifty and the threshold dose. Its bottom panel uses probit units, and she said nobody ever uses this. The threshold model has a dose below which nobody responds. The linear, nonthreshold model, a theory for carcinogens, assumes the first molecule could cause harm. Figure two dash ten is the two A A F tumor study. The bladder tumor threshold was seventy five parts per million at twenty four months and about forty five at thirty three months. Asked why it fell, she said to use the keyword cumulative. The therapeutic index is the toxic dose over the effective dose at the same percentage, usually fifty. A wide index means less chance of toxicity. The margin of safety is the toxic dose for one percent over the effective dose for ninety nine percent. Because it uses different percentages, it shows the slope of the curve, and the therapeutic index does not. The margin of exposure, for repeated exposures to something not therapeutic such as a pollutant, is the no observable adverse effect level, which she called the Noel, over the chronic exposure. That level is the highest dose with no adverse effect. In class she said lowest, which was a slip.
